rows.text: So… what does 5 × 6 actually mean?
It means 6 groups of 5. Let's put them out… one group of 5. And another. Keep going.
Now count them up… 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. So that's 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5, which is 30. And 5 × 6 means exactly the same thing.
So you don't have to count every one. Just skip count by 5s, and the 6th number you land on is the answer.
So… what does 4 × 7 actually mean?
It means 7 groups of 4. Let's put them out… one group of 4. And another. Keep going.
Now count them up… 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28. So that's 4, added 7 times, which is 28. And 4 × 7 means exactly the same thing.
Here's a shortcut. Double it, then double again. 7 doubled is 14, and 14 doubled is 28.
So… what does 20 × 3 actually mean?
It means 3 groups of 20. Let's put them out… one group of 20. And another. Keep going.
Now count them up… 20, 40, 60. So that's 20 + 20 + 20, which is 60. And 20 × 3 means exactly the same thing.
But here's a faster way. Cover up the zero… 2 × 3 is 6. Now put the zero back on… 60. Same answer, much quicker.
So… what does 1 × 7 actually mean?
It means 7 groups of 1. Let's put them out… one group of 1. And another. Keep going.
Now count them up… 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. So that's 1, added 7 times, which is 7. And 1 × 7 means exactly the same thing.
Every group has just 1 in it, so you end up with exactly what you started with. That's why anything times 1 is itself. And if there were no groups at all? Nothing. That's times 0.
So… what does 6 × 6 actually mean?
It means 6 groups of 6. Let's put them out… one group of 6. And another. Keep going.
Now count them up… 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36. So that's 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 + 6, which is 36. And 6 × 6 means exactly the same thing.
When the two numbers match, the groups make a perfect square. That's why 6 × 6 is called 6 squared.
So… what does 6 × 7 actually mean?

Now count them up… 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42. So that's 6, added 7 times, which is 42. And 6 × 7 means exactly the same thing.
Here's the trick for the hard ones. 7 × 5 is 35, and 7 more makes 42. Break it into a five you know, plus the rest.
So… what does 12 × 4 actually mean?
It means 4 groups of 12. Let's put them out… one group of 12. And another. Keep going.
Now count them up… 12, 24, 36, 48. So that's 12 + 12 + 12 + 12, which is 48. And 12 × 4 means exactly the same thing.
Split the 12. 4 × 10 is 40, and 4 × 2 is 8. Put them together… 48.
34 plus 25. Let's build it out of blocks.
34 is 3 tens and 4 ones. And 25 is 2 tens and 5 ones.
Now put all the ones together… 4 and 5 is 9. That's under ten, so nothing has to move. And the tens… 3 and 2 is 5.
So when you write it down, the columns just add straight down. 34 plus 25 is 59.
37 plus 45. Let's build it out of blocks.
37 is 3 tens and 7 ones. And 45 is 4 tens and 5 ones.

Now put all the ones together… 7 and 5 is 12. But you can't leave 12 ones in the ones column. So take ten of them… and snap them into one ten. Over it goes. That's the little 1 you carry — it was never magic, it's just ten ones that became one ten. And 2 are left behind.
So when you write it down, that little 1 above the tens is the ten you just made. 37 plus 45 is 82.

Now take away 3 ones. There are 8 up there, so that one's easy… 5 left. Nothing has to be broken apart.
So when you write it down, each column just subtracts straight down. 58 take away 23 is 35.
52 take away 27. Let's build it out of blocks.
52 is 5 tens and 2 ones. That's what we're taking from.
Now take away 7 ones. But look… there are only 2 up there. Not enough. So go next door and borrow a ten… and break it apart into ten ones. Now the ones column has 12. Take away 7, and 5 are left.
So when you write it down, that crossed-out ten is the one you broke apart. 52 take away 27 is 25.

7 plus 2. Let's use a ten-frame.
Here's 7 in the frame. And here are the other 2, waiting underneath.
Start at 7… and just count on. 8… 9.
So 7 plus 2 is 9. Start at the big number and count on.
6 plus 6. Let's use a ten-frame.
Here's 6 in the frame. And here are the other 6, waiting underneath.
The frame has 4 empty spaces. So slide 4 across… and the ten is full. That leaves 2. 10 and 2 is 12.
So 6 plus 6 is 12. Doubles are worth just knowing.

Here's 3 in the frame. And here are the other 8, waiting underneath.
3 and 8. Now watch — swap them round. 8 and 3. Same dots, just the other way about… still 11. So if you know one, you know the other.
So 3 plus 8 is 11. Swap them round — 3 + 8 is the same as 8 + 3.

The frame has 4 empty spaces. So slide 4 across… and the ten is full. That leaves 3. 10 and 3 is 13.
So 6 plus 7 is 13. 6 + 6 is 12, so one more is 13.

The frame has 2 empty spaces. So slide 2 across… and the ten is full. That leaves 3. 10 and 3 is 13.

Here's 9… filling up the frame.
Start at 9… and count back. 8… 7.

15 is a ten and 5 more. Take those 5 off first… and we're down to 10. Now 2 more to go… 8.

30 divided by 5. There are two ways to picture this, and they both give the same answer.
First way — sharing. Deal them out, one at a time, like cards… onto 5 plates. Keep going… and everyone ends up with 6.
Now the other way. Instead of sharing, ask how many 5s actually fit inside 30. Make a group of 5… and another… and count the groups. 6. Same answer.
So 30 divided by 5 is 6. 5 × 6 = 30, so 30 ÷ 5 = 6.

First way — sharing. Deal them out, one at a time, like cards… onto one plate. Keep going… and everyone ends up with 7.
Now the other way. Instead of sharing, ask how many 1s actually fit inside 7. Make a group of 1… and another… and count the groups. 7. Same answer.
So 7 divided by 1 is 7. ÷1 changes nothing.

Now the other way. Instead of sharing, ask how many 4s actually fit inside 29. Make a group of 4… and another… and count the groups. 7. And the same 1 is still stranded — not enough for a whole group.
So 29 divided by 4 is 7, remainder 1. 4 × 7 = 28, and 1 is left over.

84 is 8 tens and 4 ones. Share the tens first — 8 tens between 4… that's 2 tens each. Now the ones. 4 between 4… 1 each.
Written down it's just those two steps. 8 tens divided by 4 is 2 tens. 4 ones divided by 4 is 1. Put them together… 21.
So 84 divided by 4 is 21. Share the tens first, then the ones.
5, 8 and 13. These three belong together — and once you know how, they give you four facts for the price of one.
Here's the whole thing… 13. And it's made of two parts. 5… and 8.

Now ask the picture four different questions. Put the parts together — 5 plus 8 is 13. Swap them round — 8 plus 5 is 13. Or start from the whole and take a part away. 13 take away 8 is 5. And 13 take away 5 is 8. Same picture every time.
That's the family. Know one, and you know all four.

Now ask the picture four different questions. Put the parts together — 6 plus 9 is 15. Swap them round — 9 plus 6 is 15. Or start from the whole and take a part away. 15 take away 9 is 6. And 15 take away 6 is 9. Same picture every time.

Here it is as an array. 3 rows… with 4 in each row. That's 12 altogether.

Now ask it four questions. Count it as rows — 3 times 4 is 12. Turn it and count columns — 4 times 3 is 12. Or start from 12 and ask how many are in each row. 12 divided by 3 is 4. And 12 divided by 4 is 3. One array, four facts.
That's the family. Division asks how big one row is.

Here it is as an array. 4 rows… with 6 in each row. That's 24 altogether.

Now cut it. Across, at the tens… and down, at the tens as well. That gives four pieces, and every one of them is a fact you already know. 20 times 10 is 200. 3 times 10 is 30. 20 times 4 is 80. 3 times 4 is 12.

What does 3/4 actually mean?
Start with one whole bar. Cut it into 4 parts — and they have to be EQUAL. Same size, every one. If the parts aren't equal… it's not quarters at all.
Now shade 3 of them. One… two… three. 3 out of 4.
And that's exactly what the fraction says. The bottom number is how many equal parts. The top is how many you took. Bottom = equal parts, top = shaded parts.
Which is bigger… 3/4, or 2/3?
Two bars, exactly the same length. Cut the first into 4… and shade 3. Cut the second into 3… and shade 2.
Now line them up… and look at where the shading ends. The top bar reaches further. 3/4 is bigger.
So 3/4 is greater than 2/3. Same-length bars — the longer shading wins.
3/8 plus 2/8 — how do you add fractions?
Here's a bar cut into 8 equal parts, with 3 shaded.
Now add 2 more parts… watch them slide in. Count the shading: 5 parts.
3/8 plus 2/8 is 5/8. The bottom number didn't change — the pieces are the same size, there are just more of them. Same-size pieces just count up — the bottom stays.
4/8… can we say that more simply?
Here's 4/8 — a bar in 8 parts, 4 shaded.
Now watch the shading. Don't take your eyes off it. Erase every second cut… the parts get bigger, and now it's 2 out of 4. Erase again… 1 out of 2. And the shading? It never moved.
4/8, 2/4 and 1/2 are the SAME amount — just cut differently. Fewer, bigger pieces — the shading never changed.
0.3 and 0.03. Same thing… or not?
Here's a square cut into 100 little cells. One whole column is a tenth — ten cells. One little cell on its own is a hundredth.
0.3 is 3 whole columns… 30 cells. But 0.03 is just 3 little cells. Look at the difference. Not the same at all — one is ten times the other.
First place after the dot counts columns. Second place counts cells. 0.3 is 3 whole columns — 0.03 is just 3 little cells.
0.4 plus 0.25. Decimals… but the grid makes it easy.
0.4 is 40 cells out of 100 — shade them gold.
And 0.25 is 25 cells — shade them blue, right after. Now count everything shaded… 65 cells.
65 cells out of 100 is 0.65. So 0.4 plus 0.25 is 0.65. Line up the decimal points and add like always.
0.65 take away 0.25. Same grid… different direction.
0.65 is 65 cells out of 100 — there they are, shaded.
Now take 0.25 away — that's 25 cells, coming off… watch the count fall. 40 cells left.
40 cells is 0.4. So 0.65 take away 0.25 is 0.4. Same grid — shading comes OFF instead of going on.
0.3 × 3. Multiplying a decimal… by a whole number.
0.3 is 3 columns. That's one group.
Now take 3 groups of it… 0.3… 0.6… 0.9. 9 tenths altogether.
9 tenths is 0.9. So 0.3 × 3 is 0.9. Groups of tenths, just like groups of anything.
37 percent. What IS a percent, really?
Per cent means per hundred. So here's a hundred — a square cut into 100 cells.
Shade 37 of them… that's 37 percent. Nothing more to it.
And the same shading has three names: 37 out of 100… 0.37… and 37%. Per cent means per hundred — same number, three coats.
3 red to 2 blue. What IS a ratio?
Here's the pair. 3 red on the top row, 2 blue on the bottom.
Now multiply BOTH rows by the same number. Times 2… 6 and 4. Times 3… 9 and 6. The numbers get bigger, but the shape of the pair never changes.
3 to 2 is the same ratio as 9 to 6. Scale both sides the same, and the ratio holds.
3 over 4… equals what over 12?
Here's 3 over 4, as a table. Top row 3… bottom row 4.
Now multiply BOTH rows by the same number. Times 2… 6 and 8. Times 3… 9 and 12. The numbers get bigger, but the shape of the pair never changes.
So 3 over 4 equals 9 over 12. Same multiplier top and bottom — that's what equal means here.
12 apples for 3 pounds. What's that each?
Put it in a table. 12 apples on the top… 3 pounds underneath. That's the pair we're given.
Now scale it DOWN, until the bottom says just 1. Divide both by 3… 12 divided by 3 is 4. And 3 divided by 3 is 1.
So that's 4 apples per pound. That's the unit rate. Divide down to one — then you can compare anything.
x + 3 equals 8. What is x?
Picture a scale, sitting level. On the left: a box holding x, and 3 weights. On the right: 8 weights.
Take 3 off the left… but if you only do that, it tips. So take 3 off the RIGHT as well. Still level. Now the left is just the box, and the right is 5.
So x is 5. And you can check it — put 5 back in the box and the scale is level again. Take the same off both sides and it stays level.
2x + 3 equals 11. What is x?
Picture a scale, sitting level. On the left: 2 boxes, each holding the same x… and 3 weights. On the right: 11 weights.
First take 3 off BOTH sides… still level. Left is 2 boxes, right is 8. Now split both sides into 2… one box on the left, 4 on the right.
So x is 4. And you can check it — put 4 back in the boxes and the scale is level again. Undo the adding first, then the grouping.
x + 2 is more than 5. What can x be?
Picture a scale — but this one isn't level. The left side is HEAVIER. On the left: a box holding x, and 2 weights. On the right: 5.
Take 2 off both sides… and it's still tipped the same way. That's the thing about a tipped scale — take the same off each side and it stays tipped. Left is just the box now. Right is 3.
So x is more than 3. Not one answer — a whole range of them. A tipped scale stays tipped — same move, both sides.
Let's build y = 2x + 1 one piece at a time. Start with the simplest line there is: y equals x. Whatever number you pick… you get the same one back. Zero gives zero. One gives one. Two gives two.
Now multiply the x by 2. That's y equals 2 x. Every height gets 2 times bigger. One becomes 2… two becomes 4. Watch the line swing up — same start at zero, but steeper now.
Last piece: plus 1. Careful — adding 1 doesn't push the line sideways. It lifts every point UP, by 1. So 0, 2 and 4 become 1, 3 and 5. Same steepness… higher start.
Here's how you'd plot it from scratch. Make a table. When x is 0, y is 1. When x is 1, y is 3. When x is 2, y is 5. Each row of the table is one point on the grid.

Join the dots — perfectly straight. And here's the big idea. Every point sitting on that line is a pair that makes the equation true. The line isn't a picture of the answer. It IS the answers — all of them at once. Every point on the line is a pair that works.
This shape of equation has a name: y equals m x plus b. The m is called the slope. The b is called the y-intercept. In ours — y = 2x + 1 — the slope is 2, and the y-intercept is 1.
The y-intercept is the easy one. It's where the line cuts through the y axis — where x is zero. Look… right there, at a height of 1. That's your b.
Now the slope. Pick any two points on the line, and label them. Here's one at 1, 3… and another at 3, 7. The slope measures the climb between them.
Here's the slope formula: m equals y two minus y one… over x two minus x one. Plug in. Top: 7 minus 3 is 4. Bottom: 3 minus 1 is 2. 4 over 2… the slope is 2. Up 2 for every 1 across.
So read it at a glance. In y = 2x + 1: the 2 is m, the slope — the climb. The 1 is b, the y-intercept — where the line starts. m is the slope, b is the y-intercept.
Two equations, one puzzle. The first says y = 2x + 1. The second says y = −x + 7. Could ONE pair of numbers make both of them true… at the same time?
Take the first one. Quick table: when x is 0, y is 1. At 1, it's 3. At 2, it's 5. Plot them, join them — the blue line is every pair the first equation allows.
Now the second equation, on the same grid. Its table: at 0, it's 7. At 1, it's 6. At 2… 5. Plot, join — the gold line is every pair the SECOND one allows. Did you spot that last row?
The lines cross exactly once. That point sits on the blue line AND the gold line at the same time. x is 2… y is 5. The one pair that works for both.

Always check. First equation: 2 times 2 plus 1… 5. Yes. Second: minus 2 plus 7… 5 again. That's what solving a system means — find where the lines meet, because that pair works everywhere. One point on BOTH lines — that's the solution.
y = x² − 4. Here's the twist: squaring a number never comes out negative… so what shape will THAT make?
Work a few out. Minus 2 gives 0. Minus 1 gives -3. Zero gives -4. Now cross to the plus side… 1 gives -3 — the same as minus 1 did. And 2 gives 0 — the same as minus 2.

Join them, and it's not a line — it curves. A parabola. Fold it down the middle… the left half lands exactly on the right. That's the squaring: minus 2 and plus 2 square to the SAME number, so the picture has to mirror.
And watch where it crosses zero — twice. At -2, and at 2. Squaring makes it curve — and symmetric.
y = x² − 4. Here's a question about the WHOLE curve at once: which heights does it actually reach… and which does it never touch?
Watch the lowest point. The curve bottoms out right here, at a height of -4. That's its minimum — it can NEVER go below this line.
Now sweep upward. From -4, the two arms climb… and climb… forever. Every height from -4 on up gets touched. Everything below -4… never.
So the RANGE is: y is greater than or equal to -4. Find the vertex height, check which way the arms go — that's the whole method. Range: every height the curve actually reaches.
y = x² − 4. Forget the middle for a moment. What happens at the far EDGES — when x gets huge, or hugely negative?
Walk right. At x equals 10, x squared is 100. At 100… ten thousand. The squared term takes over everything else — the arm climbs without limit.
Now walk LEFT. x is negative… but squaring kills the sign. Minus 100, squared, is still ten thousand. So the left arm climbs too. Both ends… up.

That's end behavior: as x runs off either edge, y goes UP — because the leading term is x squared with a positive front. Even power, positive lead… both arms up. Ends point where the leading term sends them.
x² minus 5x plus 6 equals zero. You could guess numbers all day… or you could draw one picture.
Graph the left side: y = x² − 5x + 6. Now every point's height tells you what the expression is worth at that x.
And "equals zero" means: the height is zero. Where is height zero? … Exactly on the x axis. So look where the curve touches it. There… and there. At 2, and at 3.
So x is 2, or x is 3. Two crossings — two answers. Solving means finding where it crosses zero.
x² minus 5x plus 6 equals zero. You could guess numbers all day… or you could draw one picture.
Graph the left side: y = x² − 5x + 6. Now every point's height tells you what the expression is worth at that x.
And "equals zero" means: the height is zero. Where is height zero? … Exactly on the x axis. So look where the curve touches it. There… and there. At 2, and at 3.
So x is 2, or x is 3. Two crossings — two answers. The formula finds those crossings every time.
y = 2 to the power of x. That's not multiplying BY x — it's multiplying 2 by itself, x times over. What shape does that make?
Work them out. At 0 it's 1. At 1, 2. At 2, 4. At 3, 8. At 4… 16. Look at the jumps between them — they're growing.
Plot them, and watch. It barely moves at first… then it takes off. Every step across multiplies by 2 — so the bigger it is, the bigger its next jump has to be.
That's exponential growth. A straight line ADDS the same amount each step. This one MULTIPLIES. Doubling beats any straight line, eventually.
2 to the WHAT makes 8? … That question — find the exponent — has a name. It's a logarithm.
Here's y equals 2 to the x. Feed it an exponent, it hands you a value. Feed it 3… it hands you 8.
Now flip the question. Swap x and y — mirror the whole curve in the diagonal. That new curve is the log. Feed IT a value… and it hands the exponent back.
So log base 2 of 8 is 3… because 2 cubed is 8. Same relationship — just asked the other way round. A log just asks the exponent question backwards.
This function is undefined at x = 2. Nothing there at all. So… what happens right NEXT to it?
y = x² minus 4, all over x minus 2. Everywhere except 2, that cancels down to x plus 2 — a straight line. But at 2 exactly you'd be dividing by zero. So there's a hole, right there.
Walk in from the left. At 1 it's 3. At 1.5, 3.5. Closer… it's heading for 4. Now come in from the right — also heading for 4.
Both sides aim at 4. So the limit is 4 — even though the function never actually gets there. The value it heads for — even where it isn't defined.
y = x². How steep is it… exactly at x = 1? Not on average — at that one single point.
Tricky, because a curve's steepness keeps changing. So cheat a little. Pick two points, and join them. THAT line's slope is easy to measure.

Now slide the second point closer. And closer. The line swings round… and its slope settles down. When the two points are almost on top of each other, the line just touches the curve. That's the tangent.
And its slope is 2. That's the derivative at x = 1. Slope at a single point — the tangent's steepness.
How much area sits under this line, between 0 and 4? The top is slanted… so no rectangle formula fits it. Yet.
Here's y = x. The piece we want is trapped between the line and the x axis.
Chop it into rectangles. Four fat ones — that's a rough answer, sticking out in places. Now eight thinner ones… better. Now lots of very thin ones… and the gaps basically disappear.
Add up all those strips and you get 8. That's the integral. Add up the strips — that's the area underneath.

Here's a machine. Drop a number in the top… a rule works on it… and a new number slides out the bottom. Mathematicians write this machine as f(x) = 2x + 3. Strange-looking — until you know how to read it.

The letter f is just the machine's NAME. The x in the brackets is the slot where the input goes. So f of 4 means: feed 4 into machine f. Watch. 4 goes in… the rule says 2 times 4, plus 3… and out comes 11.
So when you read f of 4 equals 11, that's not algebra to solve. It's a fact: THIS machine turns 4 into 11. The brackets don't mean multiply — they mean "here's the input".
That's all function notation is. Name of the machine… input in the brackets… output on the other side of the equals sign. f(4) means: feed 4 into the machine named f.
f(x) = 3x + 2. Evaluate it at 0, at 1, and at 2. One machine… three inputs. Same moves every time.
The trick: wherever you see the x, swap in the input. Feed it 0… 3 times 0 is 0, plus 2 makes 2. Feed it 1… that's 5. And 2… 8.
Line the answers up in a table. In: 0, 1, 2. Out: 2, 5, 8. Look at the outputs — they climb by 3 every time. That's the m in m x plus b doing its job. This machine IS a line.
So evaluating a function is substitution, nothing more. Swap the x for the input… do the arithmetic… write the output. Swap the x for the input, then just do the arithmetic.
Two machines this time. Machine f adds 2. Machine g multiplies by 3. Now chain them: the output pipe of f feeds straight into g. What happens to a 2?
Follow it through. 2 drops into f… out comes 4. That 4 falls straight into g… times 3… 12. Written down, that's g of f of 2 — read it inside out, because the INSIDE machine runs first.
Now swap the machines. 2 into g first… 6. Then into f… 8. Different answer! 12 one way, 8 the other. Order matters when you chain machines.
That's composition: one machine's output becomes the next machine's input. Read the brackets from the inside out. The inside machine runs first — order matters.
f(x) = 2x + 1. Feed it 3: times 2 is 6, plus 1… 7. Now the real question: if all you know is the OUTPUT, 7… can you get back to the 3?
Run the machine backwards. Going forward it multiplied by 2, THEN added 1. So going back, undo the LAST step first: subtract 1… 6. Then divide by 2… 3. There's your input again.
That backwards machine has a name: f inverse. Notice the double reversal — opposite operations, in the opposite order. Like taking off shoes and socks: socks went on first, but they come off last.
Forward: times 2, plus 1. Inverse: minus 1, divide 2. Every step undone, in reverse. The inverse undoes each step, in reverse order.
f(x) = x² — the squaring machine. Two questions ABOUT a machine, not about any one number. What's allowed to go IN? And what can possibly come OUT?
Try some inputs. -3… squared… 9. 0… gives 0. 3… also 9. Anything can go in — positive, negative, zero. The set of allowed inputs is called the DOMAIN, and here it's every number there is.

But look at what comes out: 9, 0, 9… Can this machine EVER produce a negative? Try to imagine it — a number times itself, coming out negative. It can't. The outputs are called the RANGE, and here the range is zero and up. Never below.
Domain: every input the machine accepts. Range: every output it can actually make. Two different questions — always ask both. Domain: what can go in. Range: what can come out.
f(x) = 1 / (x − 2). A fraction machine: 1 divided by, x minus 2. Most inputs are fine… but one of them breaks this machine. Can you spot it before it happens?
Feed it 3: bottom is 3 minus 2, which is 1… output 1. Feed it 4: bottom is 2… output 0.5. Smooth so far.
Now feed it 2. Bottom: 2 minus 2… zero. And 1 divided by zero — the machine jams. There is no answer. Division by zero isn't big, isn't infinity… it's undefined.
So the domain is every number EXCEPT 2. For any fraction machine, find what makes the bottom zero — and fence it off. The domain is every input that doesn't break the machine.
A right triangle. One leg is 3, the other is 4. How long is the slanted side… without measuring it?
Build a square on each leg. The 3 side carries a square of 9. The 4 side… 16. Add the two squares together: 9 plus 16 is 25.
Now the slanted side — the hypotenuse. ITS square holds exactly 25. So the side itself is the square root of 25… which is 5. That's the Pythagorean theorem: a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
3, 4, 5 — the most famous right triangle there is. Legs squared, added… equals the hypotenuse squared. Legs squared, added — that's the hypotenuse squared.
Same triangle — 3, 4, 5. But now stand at this corner: the angle called theta. From where theta sits, every side of the triangle gets a name.
The side facing theta, across the triangle, is the OPPOSITE — here, 3. The side touching theta that isn't the slant is the ADJACENT… 4. And the slanted side is always the HYPOTENUSE… 5.
Now move theta to the other corner… and watch. Opposite and adjacent SWAP. The 4 faces the angle now. The names belong to the ANGLE, not to the triangle.
Opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse — always named from the angle you stand at. Get the names right, and the ratios later name themselves. Opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse — named from the angle.
3, 4, 5 — sides named from theta. Trigonometry is nothing but RATIOS of these sides. Three of them… each with its own name.
Sine of theta is opposite over hypotenuse: 3 over 5, which is 0.6. Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse: 4 over 5… 0.8. Tangent is opposite over adjacent: 3 over 4… 0.75.
Why care? Because the ratios depend only on the ANGLE. Blow the triangle up ten times: 30 over 50… still 0.6. Know the angle, and you know every right triangle that carries it.
Remember it as SOH CAH TOA. Sine: Opposite over Hypotenuse. Cosine: Adjacent over Hypotenuse. Tangent: Opposite over Adjacent. SOH CAH TOA — three ratios, straight from the sides.
From our triangle, sine of theta is 0.6 and cosine is 0.8. Square them both… and watch what they add up to.
0.6 squared is 0.36. 0.8 squared is 0.64. Add them: 0.36 plus 0.64… exactly 1. And that's no accident of this triangle — ANY angle lands on 1.
Here's why. Sine is 3 over 5, cosine is 4 over 5. Square and add: 9 plus 16, all over 25. But 9 plus 16 IS 25 — that's Pythagoras! So the fraction is 25 over 25. One.
Sine squared plus cosine squared equals 1 — for every angle, always. It's the Pythagorean theorem, wearing trig clothes. sin² + cos² = 1 — the theorem in disguise.
A circle with radius exactly 1, centred at zero. Walk an angle theta around from the right-hand side… and you land on a point. That point's coordinates hide all of trigonometry.
From the point, drop straight down to the x axis. That horizontal distance from the centre is the COSINE of theta. The height you dropped is the SINE. The point IS the pair: cosine, then sine.
Slide theta around and watch the pair change. Straight up, at 90 degrees: cosine 0, sine 1. Far left, at 180: cosine minus 1, sine 0. The circle turns every angle into two numbers.
Radius 1 is what makes it work: the hypotenuse is 1, so the ratios ARE the coordinates. Radius 1: the point's coordinates ARE (cos, sin).
Four compass points on the unit circle: 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees. Their sine and cosine you shouldn't have to compute — you should SEE them.
At 0 degrees the point is at 1, 0 — so cosine is 1, sine is 0. At 90, the point is 0, 1. At 180… minus 1, 0. And at 270… 0, minus 1.
See the pattern. Cosine is just the x coordinate: 1, 0, minus 1, 0. Sine is the y: 0, 1, 0, minus 1. The values trace the circle itself.
Don't memorise blind — read the point. Its coordinates ARE cosine and sine. Read the values off the axes, not from memory.
Degrees aren't the only way to measure an angle. Take the radius itself… bend it… and lay it along the rim of the circle. The angle that arc spans is called 1 RADIAN.
Keep laying radius-lengths along the circle. Halfway round takes a little more than 3 of them — exactly pi of them. So 180 degrees equals pi radians. That single fact is the whole conversion.
Everything else is a fraction of it. 90 degrees is half of 180… pi over 2. 60 degrees is a third… pi over 3. And all the way round, 360… 2 pi.
To convert any angle, multiply by pi over 180. Degrees to radians is one fact wearing different fractions: 180 degrees is pi. One fact does it all: 180° = π.
The point on the unit circle sits at cosine, sine. And EVERY point on a radius-1 circle obeys one equation: x squared plus y squared equals 1. Put those two facts together…
Swap the names in: cosine squared plus sine squared equals 1. That's the Pythagorean identity — not a rule to memorise, but the circle's own equation wearing trig names.
And it breeds more. Divide everything by cosine squared… and out falls: 1 plus tangent squared equals 1 over cosine squared. One circle, a whole family of identities.
When you forget an identity, don't guess — go back to the circle. The point at cosine, sine… radius 1. Everything grows from there. Forget one? Go back to the circle.
3 x squared, plus 2 x, minus 5. This is a polynomial — a sum of building blocks called TERMS. Classifying it takes two moves: count… and rank.
First, count. Split it at the plus and minus signs. Term one: 3 x squared. Term two: 2 x. Term three: 5. Three terms — that makes it a TRINOMIAL. One term would be a monomial. Two… a binomial.
Now rank. Look at each term's exponent on x: 2… then 1… then 0. The BIGGEST exponent is the DEGREE. Here, degree 2 — a quadratic. The degree tells you the shape of its graph before you ever draw it.

Count the terms for its name. Take the biggest exponent for its degree. 3 x squared, plus 2 x, minus 5: a trinomial of degree 2. Count the terms for the name, take the biggest exponent for the degree.
Add two polynomials: 3 x squared, plus 2 x, plus 1… and x squared, plus 4 x, plus 2. Looks heavy. It's actually just sorting.

Picture every term as a tile. Big squares for x squared… bars for x… dots for plain numbers. Pour both polynomials onto the table, and sort by SHAPE. Squares: 3 and 1 make 4. Bars: 2 and 4 make 6. Dots: 1 and 2 make 3.

And that's the one rule of the whole topic: only LIKE terms combine. A square can never merge with a bar — x squared and x are different shapes. So 4 x squared and 6 x sit side by side… and stay there.
The sum: 4 x squared, plus 6 x, plus 3. Sort by shape, add what matches, leave the rest alone. Only like terms combine — sort by shape, add what matches.
Multiply x plus 2… by x plus 3. Here's the picture that keeps it honest: a rectangle whose sides are exactly those lengths.
Split the sides. Along the top: x, then 2. Down the side: x, then 3. That cuts the rectangle into four rooms. x times x… x squared. x times 3… 3 x. 2 times x… 2 x. And 2 times 3… 6.

Collect the rooms. The x squared. Then 3 x and 2 x — like terms — together 5 x. And the 6. The product: x squared, plus 5 x, plus 6. Every term met every term. The rectangle makes missing one impossible.
Multiply every term by every term… then combine the like ones. Every term multiplies every term — the rectangle can't miss one.
x squared, plus 5 x, plus 6. Factoring asks: which two brackets MULTIPLY to make this? It's the rectangle puzzle… run backwards.
You're hunting two numbers that MULTIPLY to 6, and ADD to 5. Walk the factor pairs of 6. 1 and 6: they add to 7… no. 2 and 3: they add to 5. Yes.
So the brackets are x plus 2… and x plus 3. Don't trust it — CHECK it. Rebuild the rectangle: x squared… 3 x… 2 x… 6. Collect: x squared plus 5 x plus 6. It rebuilds perfectly.
Multiply to the last number… add to the middle one. Find that pair, and the brackets write themselves. Multiply to the last number, add to the middle one.
Factor 2 x squared, plus 7 x, plus 6. The old method was: find two numbers that multiply to the last one and add to the middle one. Try it here and it fails — because there is a 2 in front now.

One extra step fixes it. Multiply a by c: 2 times 6 is 12. NOW hunt two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7. Walk the pairs of 12: 1 and 12 add to 13, no. 2 and 6 add to 8, no. 3 and 4 add to 7. Yes.

Use them to SPLIT the middle term. 7 x becomes 3 x plus 4 x, so you have four terms: 2 x squared, plus 3 x, plus 4 x, plus 6. Now group in pairs. From the first pair take out x: that leaves x, bracket, 2 x plus 3. From the second pair take out 2: that leaves 2, bracket, 2 x plus 3. The same bracket both times — that is how you know it worked.
So it factors to, bracket, 2 x plus 3, bracket, x plus 2. Multiply a by c, split the middle, then group. Multiply a by c first - then the old trick works again.
Factor x squared minus 16. Something is missing — there is no x term at all. That absence is the clue.

Check what you have: x squared is a square, and 16 is a square, because 4 times 4 is 16. Two squares, with a MINUS between them. That pattern has its own answer: bracket, x minus 4, bracket, x plus 4.

Multiply it back and watch why the x term is missing. x times x is x squared. x times 4 is 4 x. Minus 4 times x is minus 4 x. And minus 4 times 4 is minus 16. The two middle terms are equal and opposite — they cancel every single time. That is the whole trick.
A square, minus a square, factors into the two roots subtracted and added. x squared minus 16 is x minus 4, times x plus 4. Two squares with a minus between them - the middle always cancels.
Factor x squared, plus 6 x, plus 9. You could hunt for two numbers as usual — but this one has a shape worth spotting, because it saves you the hunt entirely.
Two checks. Is the first term a square? x squared — yes, its root is x. Is the last term a square? 9 — yes, its root is 3. So the candidate is x plus 3, all squared.

Now the check that actually decides it. In a perfect square the middle term must be TWICE the two roots multiplied. The roots are x and 3. Twice their product is 2 times 3, which is 6. And the middle term IS 6 x. It matches, so it really is x plus 3, squared. If the middle had been anything else, it would just be an ordinary trinomial.
Both ends square, and the middle twice the roots multiplied. Then it is a perfect square: x plus 3, squared. Middle term is TWICE the roots multiplied - that is the test.
Factor x cubed, plus 3 x squared, plus 2 x, plus 6. Four terms this time. And nothing divides into all four, so there is no common factor to pull out.

So stop trying to factor all four at once, and split them into two pairs. First pair: x cubed plus 3 x squared. Second pair: 2 x plus 6. Factor each pair on its own. From the first, take out x squared: that leaves x squared, bracket, x plus 3. From the second, take out 2: that leaves 2, bracket, x plus 3.

Look at what appeared. Both pairs left behind the SAME bracket: x plus 3. That is not luck — it is the signal that grouping has worked. So treat that bracket as one lump and factor it out of both: x plus 3, times, bracket, x squared plus 2. If the two brackets had come out different, you would try pairing the terms a different way.
Four terms, no common factor: pair them, factor each pair, and the matching bracket comes out. Four terms, no common factor - so pair them and factor twice.
Factor x cubed plus 8. Both parts are cubes: x cubed obviously, and 8 because 2 times 2 times 2 is 8. A sum of cubes has its own formula.

Take the cube roots: x, and 2. The first bracket is simply those two added: x plus 2. The second bracket is built from the same two numbers, in three terms: the first squared, then the two multiplied, then the second squared. That gives x squared, then 2 x, then 4.

Now the signs, and there is a word for them: SOAP. Same, Opposite, Always Positive. The first bracket takes the SAME sign as the question — a plus. The middle term of the second bracket takes the OPPOSITE — a minus. And the last term is ALWAYS positive. So the answer is x plus 2, times, bracket, x squared minus 2 x plus 4. For a DIFFERENCE of cubes, only the first two signs swap over.

Cube roots first, then Same, Opposite, Always Positive. And notice the middle term is never doubled — that is what separates this from a perfect square. Same signs, opposite sign, always plus - and the middle never doubles.
Is 36 a perfect square? The name gives the answer away, if you take it literally.

A perfect square is a number of things you can arrange into an actual square — same number of rows as columns. Try it with 36. 6 rows of 6... and it fills exactly. No gaps, nothing left over. So yes, 36 is a perfect square.
And that is what a square ROOT asks: not "what is the area", but "how long is the side". The square root of 36 is 6, because 6 times 6 is 36. Root undoes squaring, the way subtracting undoes adding.
6 squared is 36, so the square root of 36 is 6. Squaring gives the area; rooting gives the side. A perfect square really is a square you can build.
Solve x squared equals 9. Most people say 3 straight away — and they are right, but they are only half right.
Check 3: 3 squared is 9. That works. Now check negative 3. negative 3 times negative 3... a negative times a negative is a positive, so that is 9 as well. It works too.

Squaring throws the sign away. 3 and negative 3 both land on 9, so when you undo it there is no way to tell which one you started from — and you have to keep both. x equals plus or minus 3. Missing the negative is the single most common lost mark in this topic.
x squared equals 9 gives x equals plus or minus 3. Take the square root of both sides, and write BOTH answers. Squaring hides the sign, so the answer comes back in a pair.
Simplify the square root of 8. 8 is not a perfect square, so this will not come out as a whole number — but it can still be tidied.
Look for a perfect square hiding inside 8. Its factor pairs: 1 and 8, then 2 and 4. And 4 IS a perfect square. So write the root of 8 as the root of 4, times the root of 2.

Now the root of 4 is exactly 2, so it walks out from under the root sign. The root of 2 has no square factors left, so it stays. The answer is 2 root 2. Same value as before — the root of 8 is about 2 point 8, and so is 2 root 2 — just written honestly.
Split off the biggest perfect square, take its root outside, leave the rest under. Root 8 is 2 root 2. Split off the biggest perfect square, then walk it out.
Solve, bracket, x minus 3, bracket, x minus 5, equals zero. Two things multiplied together give zero. What does that force?

Think about ordinary numbers. If two numbers multiply to make 12, you know almost nothing — it could be 3 and 4, or 2 and 6. But if two numbers multiply to make ZERO, you know something enormous: at least one of them must BE zero. Nothing else works.

So one of the brackets is zero. Either x minus 3 is zero, which means x is 3. Or x minus 5 is zero, which means x is 5. Two brackets, two answers: 3 and 5. And this only works because the other side is zero — if it said 12, none of this reasoning would hold.
A product is zero only if a factor is zero. Set each bracket to zero in turn. x equals 3, or 5. Zero is the only number that forces a factor to be zero.
Solve x squared minus 9 x plus 18 equals zero. It is already set to zero, which is exactly the shape you need.

Factor the left side. Hunt two numbers that MULTIPLY to 18 and ADD to 9. Both signs come out negative, since they multiply to a positive and add to a negative. Try 3 and 6: 3 times 6 is 18, and 3 plus 6 is 9. That is the pair.

So it factors to, bracket, x minus 3, bracket, x minus 6, equals zero. Now the zero-product property finishes it: x is 3, or x is 6. Check the first: 3 squared is 9, minus 9 times 3 which is 27, plus 18. That comes to zero.
Zero on one side, factor the other, then set each bracket to zero. x equals 3 or 6. Get zero on one side, factor, then read off the roots.
x squared plus 4 x plus 6 equals zero. Before you spend any time solving it, you can find out whether it HAS a solution at all.

The discriminant is the part of the quadratic formula that lives under the square root: b squared minus 4 a c. Here a is 1, b is 4, c is 6. So b squared is 16. And 4 a c is 24. Take them: 16 minus 24 is negative 8.

Negative. And that number sits under a square root — you cannot take the square root of a negative and get a real number. So there are NO real solutions. On a graph that means the parabola floats entirely above the x axis and never touches it. If the discriminant had been positive you would get two solutions; exactly zero would give one.

b squared minus 4 a c: positive gives two solutions, zero gives one, negative gives none. Here it is negative 8, so there are no real solutions. The discriminant counts the answers before you find them.
3 x minus 4 equals 11. Two things have happened to x: it was multiplied by 3, and then 4 was taken off. To get x back on its own, you undo both — but the ORDER matters.

Think about getting dressed. Socks first, then shoes. To undo it you take the shoes off first — the LAST thing done is the FIRST thing undone. Here, the last thing done to x was taking 4 away. So undo that first: add 4. To both sides, always. 11 plus 4 is 15, so now 3 x equals 15.
One step left. x is multiplied by 3, so divide by 3 — both sides again. 15 divided by 3 is 5. x equals 5. And check it, always: 3 times 5 is 15, take away 4... 11. That is what we were told.
Undo the adding and subtracting first, then the multiplying and dividing. Reverse order, both sides, every time. Undo in reverse order - the last thing done is the first thing undone.
3, bracket, x plus 4, equals 21. Most people reach straight for the distributive property here. You can — but there is something quicker sitting in front of you.

Look at what the bracket IS: one lump, and it has been multiplied by 3. So divide both sides by 3 and the bracket is free. 21 divided by 3 is 7. Now it reads: x plus 4 equals 7. Take 4 off both sides, and x equals 3.

Now do it the other way, to prove they agree. Expand: 3 times x is 3 x, and 3 times 4 is 12. So 3 x plus 12 equals 21. Take 12 off both sides: 3 x equals 9. Divide by 3: x equals 3. The same answer, by a longer road.

If the number outside divides the number on the right neatly, divide FIRST — it is fewer steps and fewer mistakes. If it does not, expand instead. A bracket times a number can be undone by dividing first.
5 x plus 2 equals 2 x plus 11. There are x's on both sides now, and that feels like a new kind of problem. It is not. It is the same balance.

You have been moving numbers across for ages: take the same amount off both sides, and the balance holds. x's are no different. Take 2 x off BOTH sides. On the left, 5 x minus 2 x leaves 3 x. On the right, the 2 x is gone entirely — just 11 left.
So 3 x plus 2 equals 11. Now it is an ordinary two-step equation. Take 2 off both sides: 11 minus 2 is 9, so 3 x equals 9. Divide by 3: x equals 3.

Collect the x's on one side and the plain numbers on the other, then finish as normal. Check it: 5 times 3 plus 2, and 2 times 3 plus 11 — both come to 17. Move the x's to one side the same way you move numbers.
x over 4 equals 6. A fraction in an equation looks like trouble, but read what it actually says: some number, cut into 4 equal parts, and one of those parts is 6.

Said that way you can almost answer it out loud. If one part out of 4 is 6, then the whole thing is 4 lots of 6. And that is exactly what the algebra does: x has been DIVIDED by 4, so undo it by MULTIPLYING by 4.
Multiply both sides by 4. On the left, the 4 on the bottom and the 4 you multiplied by cancel — leaving just x. On the right, 6 times 4 is 24. So x equals 24. Check: 24 divided by 4 is 6. Correct.
Dividing is undone by multiplying, on BOTH sides. x over 4 equals 6 means x equals 24. Divided by 4 is undone by multiplying by 4.
The point 3, 2. A transformation moves it somewhere new — but never randomly. Each one is a rule you can apply to the two coordinates, and there are three worth knowing.

First, reflect across the x axis. The x axis is a mirror lying flat. Across is a straight drop, so the across-value does not change — still 3. The up-value flips to the other side: 2 becomes negative 2. The image is 3, negative 2. Reflect in the y axis instead and it is the other way round: negative 3, 2.

Second, translate — a slide, with no turning and no flipping. Slide by 2 across and negative 1 up: just add them on. 3 plus 2 is 5, and 2 plus negative 1 is 1. That is 5, 1. Third, rotate a quarter turn anticlockwise about the origin: the coordinates swap and the new first one changes sign. 3, 2 becomes negative 2, 3.
Reflect flips one coordinate. Translate adds to both. A quarter turn swaps them and changes a sign. Every transformation is one rule applied to the coordinates.
x plus 7. That is not a puzzle with one answer — it is a RULE. It says: take a number, and add 7 to it. Until someone tells you what x is, there is nothing to work out.
So here it comes: x is 4. Now the letter has a value, and you can swap it in. Wherever you see x, write 4 instead. x plus 7 becomes 4 plus 7... which is 11.

Now watch what makes this different from ordinary sums. Change x. Say x is 10. The rule has not changed at all — still add 7 — but the answer has: 10 plus 7 is 17. One expression, and a different answer for every x you feed it.
Substitute, then work it out. A minus behaves exactly the same way: x minus 7, when x is 4, is negative 3. An expression is a rule - feed it a number, get a number back.
3 x. Two symbols squashed together with no sign between them — and that is exactly what makes people read it wrong.
It does not mean 3 next to x, and it does not mean 3 PLUS x. When a number sits against a letter, the multiply sign is simply hidden. 3 x means 3 TIMES x. Say it that way in your head every time.
So let x be 4. That gives you 3 groups, each holding 4. Count them: 4... 8... 12. And if x were 10, you would have 3 groups of 10 — that is 30.
A number touching a letter means multiply. 3 x, when x is 4, is 12. 3x is 3 TIMES x - the multiply sign is just hiding.
Simplify 3 x plus 2 x. It looks like algebra, but you already know how to do it — you just have to see what x really is.

Treat x as a THING. A box. 3 x is 3 boxes. 2 x is 2 boxes. Push them together and you are holding 3 boxes plus 2 boxes... 5 boxes. So 3 x plus 2 x is 5 x. The x never changes — only how many of them you have.

Now the part that catches people out. What about 3 x plus 2? A plain 2 is not 2 boxes — it is just 2. Different things do not combine. 3 x plus 2 stays as 3 x plus 2, and that IS the answer. It is not unfinished.
Only terms with the same letter add together. Add the numbers in front, keep the x. Count the x's. Plain numbers are a different thing entirely.
Expand 3, bracket, x plus 4. It means 3 lots of everything inside — and the way to never forget the second bit is to draw it.

Picture a rectangle 3 tall. Its width is x plus 4, so cut the width into two pieces: a piece of length x, and a piece of length 4. Two rooms. The first room is 3 times x, which is 3 x. The second is 3 times 4, which is 12.

Add the rooms: 3 x plus 12. Now check it. Let x be 5. The original: 5 plus 4 is 9, and 3 times 9 is 27. The expansion: 3 times 5 is 15, plus 12... 27. Both 27. It really is the same rectangle, counted two ways.
The number outside multiplies EVERY term inside. 3, bracket, x plus 4, is 3 x plus 12. The number outside reaches every term inside.
Solve 4 x equals 12. Read it as a sentence first: 4 identical boxes weigh 12 altogether. What is in one box?
Picture a balance. On the left, 4 boxes, all the same. On the right, 12. It is level, so the two sides really are equal — and they will stay equal as long as you treat both sides the same.
So share both sides into 4 equal parts. The left becomes one box. The right, 12 shared between 4, is 3. One box holds 3. x equals 3. Check it: 4 times 3 is 12. Balanced.
x was multiplied by 4, so divide by 4 to undo it — on BOTH sides. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
negative 1, minus 4. Negative numbers feel strange on paper. On a number line they stop being strange, because plus and minus turn into directions.

Here is the rule, and it is the whole topic. Plus means walk RIGHT. Minus means walk LEFT. And you always start standing on the first number. So find negative 1 — 1 step left of zero — and stand there.

Now the minus tells you which way: left. And the 4 tells you how far. Walk 4 steps left. negative 2... negative 3... negative 4... negative 5. You land on negative 5. Going left past zero is not a special case — it is just carrying on walking.
negative 1 minus 4 is negative 5. Stand on the first number, let the sign point the way, and walk. Plus walks right, minus walks left - start where the first number is.
3 x squared, plus 5 x, minus 2. Before you can DO anything to a polynomial, you have to be able to read it — and reading it starts with putting it in order.

Every term carries a power of x. 3 x squared carries exponent 2. 5 x carries exponent 1. And the last term, negative 2? Exponent 0 — it has no x at all. Standard form means: line them up with the biggest exponent FIRST, then down. 2... then 1... then 0.

Now every part has a name. The biggest exponent, 2, is the DEGREE. The number sitting in front of that leading term, 3, is the LEADING COEFFICIENT. And the term with no x, negative 2, is the CONSTANT TERM — constant because it never changes when x does.

Sort by exponent, biggest first. Then the front number is the leading coefficient, the top exponent is the degree, and the lonely number on the end is the constant. Highest power first - then every part has a name.
3 x squared, plus 5 x, minus 2. Right now x is a question mark. Evaluating means someone finally tells you: x is 2. So what is the polynomial worth?
Swap every x for 2 — every single one. 3 times 2 squared... plus 5 times 2... minus 2. Powers go first: 2 squared is 4. So that first term is 3 times 4, which is 12.
The middle term: 5 times 2 is 10. Now add them up. 12, plus 10, minus 2... 20. Careful here — 3 times 2 squared does NOT mean square the 3. The exponent belongs to the x, and nothing else.
Substitute the number in for x, do the powers first, then the multiplying, then the adding. At x equals 2, this polynomial is worth 20. A polynomial is a recipe: put the number in, work it out.
Take 5 x squared, plus 3 x, plus 7... and subtract 2 x squared, plus 4 x, plus 1. This is where more marks are lost than anywhere else in the topic — and it is all down to one sign.

The minus is not just in front of the 2 x squared. It is in front of the whole BRACKET, so it hits every term inside. Flip them all: minus 2 x squared, minus 4 x, minus 1. That plus 4 x became a minus.

Now it is just adding, and adding is sorting by shape. Squared terms: 5 take away 2 is 3. The x terms: 3 take away 4... negative 1. Yes, negative — that is allowed. And the plain numbers: 7 take away 1 is 6.
The answer: 3 x squared, minus x, plus 6. Give the minus to EVERY term in the second bracket, then combine like terms as usual. The minus applies to EVERY term in the second bracket.
3 x times 4 x squared. Two single terms — monomials. They multiply, but the coefficients and the exponents behave completely differently.
Split the job in two. The plain numbers out front: 3 times 4, which is 12. Then the x parts. And here is the thing people get wrong — you do NOT multiply the exponents.

Write out what the letters actually mean. An x on its own is a single x. x squared is x times x. Push them together and you are multiplying 3 x's in a row — that is x cubed. So exponents ADD: 1 plus 2 is 3. The answer: 12 x cubed.
Multiply the coefficients, ADD the exponents. 3 times 4 is 12; 1 plus 2 is 3. Coefficients multiply; exponents ADD.
6 x squared, plus 4 x, all divided by 2 x. One long fraction. The trick is to stop seeing it as one.
A sum on top can be split up. 6 x squared over 2 x... PLUS 4 x over 2 x. Two small easy divisions instead of one frightening one.

Take the first. Numbers: 6 divided by 2 is 3. Letters: x squared divided by x — cancel one x from the top against one on the bottom, and a single x is left. So 3 x. The second: 4 divided by 2 is 2, and the x cancels away completely, leaving just 2.
The answer: 3 x plus 2. Split the fraction term by term, divide the numbers, and SUBTRACT the exponents. Split the fraction term by term, then subtract exponents.
6 x squared, plus 9 x. Factoring out the greatest common factor asks a simple question: what does every term here have in common?

Check the numbers first. What divides both 6 and 9? 3. Now the letters: 6 x squared has an x in it, and 9 x has an x in it, so both share at least one x. Put those together and the greatest common factor is 3 x.

Pull it out to the front and ask what is left behind. From 6 x squared, taking 3 x leaves 2 x. From 9 x, it leaves 3. So the answer is 3 x, bracket, 2 x plus 3. Check it by multiplying back out: 6 x squared plus 9 x. It rebuilds.
Find what every term shares — numbers and letters — put it out front, and write what is left in the bracket. Multiply back to check. Factoring out is distributing, run backwards.
5 x, bracket, x, plus 4. One term outside, a bracket inside. The outside term has to reach EVERY term in there — and the way to make sure it does is a rectangle.

Draw it 5 x tall, with the width split into x and 4. Two rooms. First room: 5 x times x — coefficients multiply, exponents add — that is 5 x squared. Second room: 5 x times 4 is 20 x. So the answer is 5 x squared plus 20 x.

Now a trinomial: x squared, plus 3 x, plus 2. Three terms inside instead of two. Watch what changes about the method... nothing. The rectangle simply gets a third room. 5 x cubed. Then 15 x squared. Then 10 x. However many terms are in the bracket, that is how many rooms you draw.
One room per term inside. Multiply the coefficients, add the exponents, and never leave a room empty. Every term in the bracket gets multiplied - no exceptions.
x squared, plus 5 x, plus 6, divided by x plus 2. This looks like a new skill. It is the long division you learned with numbers, with x's along for the ride.

Three steps, on repeat: divide, multiply, subtract. Divide: what times x gives x squared? x. So x is the first piece of the answer. Multiply: x times x plus 2 is x squared plus 2 x. Subtract that from the top. The x squared cancels, and 5 x take away 2 x leaves 3 x.

Bring down the 6, and go round again. Divide: what times x gives 3 x? 3. Multiply: 3 times x plus 2 is 3 x plus 6. Subtract... nothing left. A remainder of zero, which tells you x plus 2 was a factor all along. The answer is x plus 3.
Divide, multiply, subtract, bring down — then repeat until nothing is left. Same steps as long division with numbers - divide, multiply, subtract.
5/8, take away 2/8. The pieces are the SAME size... so this is easier than it looks.
Here's 5/8: a bar cut into 8 equal parts, with 5 of them shaded.
Now take 2 of those shaded pieces away... watch them go. Count what's left: 3 pieces. And they're still 8ths - taking pieces away never changes the size of a piece.
5/8 minus 2/8 is 3/8. Same-size pieces: subtract the tops... and the bottom stays. Same-size pieces: subtract the tops, the bottom stays.
1/2 times 3/4. Here's the secret: times means OF. This asks for half OF three quarters.
Start with the 3/4: a square cut into 4 columns, with 3 of them shaded.
Now take 1/2 of THAT. Cut everything into 2 rows... and keep just 1 row of the shading. Count: 3 pieces survive, out of 8 in the whole square.
So 1/2 times 3/4 is 3/8. Tops multiply: 1 times 3 is 3. Bottoms multiply: 2 times 4 is 8. Times means OF - tops multiply, bottoms multiply.
3/4 divided by 1/4. Division asks a fitting question: how many 1/4 pieces fit inside 3/4?
Here's 3/4: 3 shaded quarters. And here's the measuring piece: a single 1/4.
Lay the measuring piece onto the shading, and count the fits. One... two... three. It fits exactly 3 times.
3/4 divided by 1/4 is 3. And look: that's the same answer as 3/4 times 4/1 - flip the second fraction, then multiply. Division asks: how many of these fit in that?.
One and 3/4. A whole number and a fraction, written together - that's called a MIXED number. How much is it, really?
Two bars, cut into 4ths. The first is completely full - that's the 1, a whole bar. The second has 3 parts shaded - that's the 3/4.
Now count EVERYTHING in 4ths. The full bar holds 4 of them... plus the 3 in the second bar... 7 4ths altogether.
So one and 3/4 is the same amount as 7/4. Mixed numbers are for reading; the fraction form is for calculating. A whole and a fraction, living together.
7/4. Look at the top - it's BIGGER than the bottom. Can a fraction be more than a whole? ... It can.
Here are 7 loose pieces, each one a 4th of a bar.
Start filling. 4 of them fill one whole bar, edge to edge... and the 3 left over fill 3 parts of the next bar.
So 7/4 is 1 whole and 3/4. A top bigger than the bottom isn't a mistake - it just means more than one whole. Top bigger than bottom just means more than one whole.
Three fractions: 3/8, 1/2, and 3/4. Which is smallest... and which is biggest?
Give each one a bar - all three bars exactly the same length. Cut each bar by its own bottom number, and shade its top number of parts.
Now just READ the shading. 3/8 reaches the shortest distance... 1/2 reaches further... and 3/4 reaches the furthest of all.
Smallest to biggest: 3/8, then 1/2, then 3/4. Never compare the numbers alone - compare how far the shading reaches. Same-length bars turn ordering into looking.
Which is bigger: 0.3, or 0.25? Careful - 0.25 has MORE digits. Most people guess wrong here.
Put each one on a hundred square. 0.3 is 30 cells out of 100. 0.25 is 25 cells.
Now look at them side by side. 30 cells... against 25. The one with FEWER digits covers more of the square.
So 0.3 is bigger than 0.25. Extra digits mean smaller pieces, not a bigger number. More digits does not mean bigger - line them up and look.
Round 0.67 to the nearest tenth. Which tenth is it closest to?
Here's a number line from 0.6 to 0.7. Those are the two tenths on either side of it. Now find 0.67 - it sits between them.
Look at the midpoint, halfway between. 0.67 is PAST the middle... so it's nearer to 0.7 than to 0.6.
So 0.67 rounds to 0.7. Forget the rules about digits - just ask which mark it's nearer to. Which mark is it nearer? That is the whole rule.
0.3 times 0.4. Here's the surprise: the answer is SMALLER than both of them. Watch why.
Take a whole square and shade 0.3 of it - that's 3 columns out of 10.
Now take 0.4 OF that shading. Cut the square the other way into 10 rows, and keep 4 of them. Count where the two shadings overlap: 12 little squares out of 100.
12 out of 100 is 0.12. So 0.3 times 0.4 is 0.12. Taking a PART of a part always leaves you less. Multiplying by less than one makes it smaller.
0.8 divided by 0.2. Same question as always: how many 0.2s fit inside 0.8?
0.8 is 80 cells of the hundred square. And 0.2 is 20 cells - that's the piece we're measuring with.
Now cut the 80 into groups of 20. One... two... three... four. It fits exactly 4 times.
So 0.8 divided by 0.2 is 4. Notice the answer is bigger than what you started with - that happens whenever you divide by less than one. Division asks how many fit - decimals are no different.
0.3 plus 0.25. One has a single digit after the point, the other has two - and that is exactly where people go wrong, because they line up the ENDS of the numbers.
The grid settles it. 0.3 is 30 cells of the hundred square - 30 hundredths. 0.25 is 25 cells. Written as 30 hundredths and 25 hundredths, they are the same KIND of thing, and you can just add them.
30 cells plus 25 cells is 55 cells. That is 55 hundredths, which is 0.55. On paper you get there by lining up the decimal POINTS, one under the other, and letting the columns sort themselves out.
0.3 plus 0.25 is 0.55. Subtracting works the same way: 30 cells take away 25 cells is 5 cells, so 0.3 minus 0.25 is 0.05. Line up the decimal points, not the ends of the numbers.
1.2 divided by 3. This one is different from dividing by a decimal. Dividing by a whole number is SHARING: split 1.2 equally between 3.
Counting in tenths makes it easy. 1.2 is 12 tenths. And 12 is a number you already know how to share.
12 tenths shared between 3 gives 4 tenths each. 4 tenths is 0.4. So 1.2 divided by 3 is 0.4.
Share the tenths, then write the answer in tenths again. The decimal point stays exactly where it was - it does not slide about. Share the tenths out - the point does not move.
What is 20 percent of 60? Percent means per hundred, so this asks for 20 hundredths of 60.
Split 60 into 100 equal shares. Each share is worth 0.6.
Now take 20 of those shares. 20 shares, each worth 0.6... that comes to 12.
So 20 percent of 60 is 12. The quick way: turn the percent into a decimal and multiply. 20 percent is 0.2, and 0.2 times 60 is 12. Percent means per hundred, so 20% is 20 hundredths of it.
Something costs 40, and the price goes UP by 25 percent. What's the new price?
First find the change itself. 25 percent of 40... that's 10.
Now add it on. 40 plus 10 is 50. And if the price had DROPPED by 25 percent instead, you'd take the same 10 off: 40 minus 10 is 30.
Up 25 percent gives 50. Down 25 percent gives 30. Always find the part first, then decide whether it goes on or comes off. Find the part first, then add it on or take it off.
47. Two digits... but they do not mean the same thing. What does the 4 really stand for?
Here are 47 ones, all loose. Far too many to count safely. So bundle them: every ten ones snap together into one rod.
Count the rods. One... two... three... 4. 4 rods, and 7 ones left over that could not make a full ten.
So the 4 in 47 is not 4 — it is 4 TENS, which is 40. The left digit counts the BUNDLES of ten.
47 again. This time look at the other digit — the 7 on the right. What is it counting?
Here is 47 in blocks: 4 rods of ten, and some loose ones beside them.
Count only the loose ones. 7. They are the leftovers — there were not enough of them to bundle into another ten.
So 47 is 40 plus 7. The left digit counts bundles of ten; the right digit counts singles. The right digit counts the loose ones.
Which is bigger: 43, or 38?
Build them both. 43 is 4 rods and 3 ones. 38 is 3 rods and 8 ones.
Now look at the RODS first, not the ones. 4 rods against 3. That is already 10 more, and no pile of loose ones can catch up — you would need ten of them just to make one more rod.
So 43 is bigger than 38. Compare the tens first. Only if the tens are equal do you look at the ones. Tens decide it first - only check ones if the tens tie.
Counting by 2. Instead of every single number, we take bigger hops — and land on the same numbers every time.
Here is a number line, starting at 0. Each hop is exactly 2 long. Same size, every hop.
Off we go. 2... 4... 6... 8... 10... keep hopping.
2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16. Same size hop, every time. Counting by 2 gets you there far faster than counting by one.
Counting by 10. Instead of every single number, we take bigger hops — and land on the same numbers every time.
Here is a number line, starting at 0. Each hop is exactly 10 long. Same size, every hop.
Off we go. 10... 20... 30... 40... 50... keep hopping.
10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60. Only the tens digit changes. Counting by 10 gets you there far faster than counting by one.
What number comes just BEFORE 60?
Find 60 on the number line. Before means to the LEFT — the direction numbers get smaller.
Take one step left... and you land on 59. One step the other way, to the right, would be 61 — that is the number AFTER.
So 59 comes before 60, and 61 comes after. One step BACK is one less.
Put these in order: minus 3… then 5… then minus 1… then 2. Minus signs make it feel tricky… until you put them on a number line.
Every integer has an address on the line. Minus 3 sits three steps LEFT of zero. Minus 1, just one step left. Then 2 and 5 on the right. Place them all… and look.
The line has already sorted them. Further LEFT means smaller — so minus 3 is the smallest, even though 3 feels bigger than 1. It's further from zero on the cold side.
In order: minus 3… then minus 1… then 2… then 5. Further left on the line means smaller — minus signs and all.
3 plus 4 times 2. Two students solve it. One gets 14… the other gets 11. They can't both be right. Who is?
The first went left to right: 3 plus 4 is 7, times 2… 14. The second followed the RULE: multiplication first. 4 times 2 is 8… THEN add 3… 11.

11 is correct. Multiplication and division always go before addition and subtraction — that's the agreement that makes maths mean one thing. Want the other answer? You need brackets: 3 plus 4, in brackets, times 2… THAT'S 14.
Brackets first… then powers… then multiply and divide… then add and subtract. One expression, one meaning. Multiply and divide before you add and subtract.
3 plus 2 i. A number with an i in it — imaginary. Scary name… but here's the secret: it's just a POINT.
Give numbers a second direction. The real part, 3, goes ACROSS. The imaginary part, 2, goes UP. So 3 plus 2 i lives at the point 3 across, 2 up. Every complex number is an address on this plane.
And adding is easy. Add 1 plus 1 i: across parts together, 3 plus 1 is 4. Up parts together, 2 plus 1 is 3. The answer: 4 plus 3 i. Reals with reals… imaginaries with imaginaries.
A complex number is a point: real part across, imaginary part up. a + bi is a point: a across, b up.
3… then 7… then 11… then 15… What's the pattern — and what comes next?
Check the gaps. 3 to 7: plus 4. 7 to 11: plus 4 again. The same hop every time — that's an ARITHMETIC sequence. So the next term is 15 plus 4… 19.
Now the second idea. ADD the terms up as you go: 3… then 10… then 21… then 36. That running total is called a SERIES. Same numbers — different question.
A sequence is the list. A series is the sum. Find the hop first — everything else follows. A sequence lists the terms; a series adds them up.
A vector is an arrow: it has a direction, and a length. This one goes 3 across and 2 up. Write it as 3, 2. What happens when arrows ADD?
Add the arrow 1, 3. The rule is tip to tail: start the second arrow where the first one ENDS. Walk the first arrow… then walk the second… and you land at 4, 5.
Now check the shortcut. Across: 3 plus 1 is 4. Up: 2 plus 3 is 5. The components just ADD. One straight arrow from start to finish — same answer, no drawing needed.
An arrow with direction and length… added tip to tail… or component by component. Add tip-to-tail — the components just add.
The derivative measures how fast a function climbs. For powers of x there's a rule so clean it feels like a magic trick… and it's two moves long.
Take x to the power 3. Move one: bring the exponent DOWN in front. Move two: drop the exponent by one. So the derivative of x cubed is… 3 x squared. That's the whole rule.
Again, faster. x to the power 5: bring down the 5… drop to 4… the derivative is 5 x to the power 4. Any power, same two moves.
The derivative of x to the n… is n, times x to the n minus 1. Down in front… drop by one. Bring the exponent down, then drop it by one.
5 x cubed. A coefficient in front now. Does the power rule still work… and what happens to the 5?
The 5 just rides along. Power rule on the x cubed: bring down the 3, drop to 2… that's 3 x squared. Then the coefficient multiplies: 5 times 3 is 15.
So the derivative of 5 x cubed is 15 x squared. One clean habit: multiply coefficient by exponent… then lower the exponent by one. Try it on any monomial — it never changes.
Coefficient times exponent in front… exponent drops by one. The coefficient rides along and multiplies.
Why learn derivatives at all? Here's the honest answer. A ball rolls, and its distance after t seconds is t squared metres. How FAST is it moving at 3 seconds?
Speed is how fast distance changes — and that's exactly what a derivative measures. Power rule on t squared: bring down the 2… drop to 1… the speed is 2 t.
Now it's arithmetic. At 3 seconds, the speed is 2 times 3… 6 metres per second. Not the average speed — the speed at that exact instant. That's what the derivative bought us.
Position… differentiate… speed. The derivative turns "where is it" into "how fast". The derivative of position is speed.
Where does 2 x squared, plus 2 x, minus 3 cross the y axis? It sounds like it needs a graph. It needs one number.

Every point on the y axis has the same across-value: zero. So the y-intercept is simply what the polynomial is worth when x is zero. Put zero in. 2 times zero squared is zero. 2 times zero is zero. Both terms vanish.

All that survives is the constant: minus 3. So the curve crosses at zero, minus 3. And that is true for every polynomial ever written — the constant term IS the y-intercept, sitting in plain sight at the end of the expression.
Set x to zero and read off the constant. Here the y-intercept is minus 3. The y-intercept is just f of zero.
Take f of x equals, bracket, x minus 2, squared, times, bracket, x plus 3. Its roots are 2 and minus 3. But the graph does something different at each one.
Count how many times each root appears. The x minus 2 factor is SQUARED, so 2 appears twice — multiplicity 2. The other factor appears once, so minus 3 has multiplicity 1.

That count decides the shape. An EVEN multiplicity means the curve touches the axis and turns back — it bounces. So at 2, it bounces. An ODD multiplicity means it passes straight through. So at minus 3, it crosses. Even bounces, odd crosses.
Count the repeats of each factor. Even, and it bounces; odd, and it crosses. Even multiplicity bounces; odd multiplicity crosses.
A polynomial of degree 4. How many times can its graph change direction — go from climbing to falling, or falling to climbing?

Those changes are called turning points. Think about the shapes you already know. A straight line, degree 1, never turns. A parabola, degree 2, turns exactly once, at its vertex. Degree 3 can turn twice — up, down, up.

The pattern is one less than the degree, every time. So degree 4 can turn at most 3 times. At MOST — it might turn fewer times, but it can never turn more. The degree sets a ceiling on how wiggly the curve is allowed to be.
Degree 4 means at most 3 turning points. Take one off the degree. At most one fewer turn than the degree.
A polynomial of degree 9. How many roots does it have? Not "how many can you find" — how many ARE there?
The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra answers it exactly: a polynomial of degree 9 has exactly 9 roots. Not at most. Exactly. But that promise comes with two pieces of small print.

First, you must count repeats. If a factor appears twice, that root counts twice. Second, you must allow COMPLEX roots — the ones with i in them. Once you count that way, the number is always exactly the degree. A degree 9 polynomial has exactly 9 roots, however hidden some of them are.
Degree 9, exactly 9 roots — counting multiplicity, and counting complex ones. Degree n means exactly n roots, counting multiplicity.
Divide 2 x squared, plus 2 x, minus 3, by x minus 2. Long division works. Synthetic division does the same job with nothing but the numbers.
Write the coefficients in a row: 2, then 2, then minus 3. Put 2 outside — that is the root that makes x minus 2 zero. Now: bring down the 2. Multiply by 2: 4. Add it to the 2: 6.
Repeat, exactly the same. Multiply 6 by 2: 12. Add it to minus 3: 9. And you are done. The numbers along the bottom, 2 and 6, are the quotient — 2 x plus 6. The last one, 9, is the remainder.
Bring down, multiply, add — then repeat. The final number is the remainder: 9. Bring down, multiply, add - and the last number is the remainder.
You need a root of a polynomial and there is no formula to hand. Guessing at random could take all day. The Rational Root Theorem tells you the only guesses worth making.

It says: any rational root must be a factor of the CONSTANT term, divided by a factor of the LEADING coefficient. Here the constant is 15 and the leading coefficient is 1. Factors of 15: 1, then 3, then 5, then 15.

The leading coefficient is 1, and its only factor is 1 — so the bottom of the fraction never changes anything. That leaves plus or minus 1, 3, 5, and 15. Eight candidates instead of infinity. Now test them, and 3 is one that works.
Factors of the constant over factors of the leading coefficient — that is your entire list of suspects. Possible roots are factors of the constant over factors of the leading coefficient.
Solve 3 to the power x equals 27. The x is stuck up in the exponent, where none of your usual moves reach it.
So bring the two sides into the same language. 27 is not just a number here — it is a power of 3. 3 times 3 is 9, times 3 again is 27. So 27 is 3 cubed.
Rewrite it: 3 to the power x equals 3 to the power 3. Now both sides are the same base, raised to something. If the bases match, the exponents have no choice but to match too. x equals 3.
Write both sides as powers of the same base, then set the exponents equal. Same base means the exponents must match.
i is the number whose square is minus 1. Raise it to higher and higher powers and something surprising happens — it starts going round in circles.

Work up from the bottom. i to the power 1 is just i. i squared is minus 1, by definition. i cubed is i squared times i, which is minus 1 times i… minus i. And i to the power 4 is i squared times i squared: minus 1 times minus 1… 1.

Back to 1 — exactly where you started. So the next one, i to the power 5, is i again, and the whole thing repeats every 4 steps. That is the shortcut: to find any power of i, divide the exponent by 4 and keep only the remainder.
i, then minus 1, then minus i, then 1 — and round again. Divide the power by 4 and use what is left over. The powers of i repeat every four.
A geometric sequence starts at 2, with a ratio of 3. Find term 3. The word "ratio" is the clue to what makes this different.

In the sequences you met first, you ADD the same amount each step. Here you MULTIPLY by the same amount each step. Start at 2. Times 3 gives 6. Times 3 again gives 18. So the sequence runs 2… then 6… then 18.

Term 3 is 18. But notice how you got there: you multiplied by 3 twice, not 3 times. To reach term 3 you take 3 minus 1 steps. So the rule is: the first term, times the ratio, raised to one less than the term number.
Multiply, do not add. Term 3 of this sequence is 18. Each term MULTIPLIES by the ratio.
The limit, as x approaches 4, of x squared plus x plus 2. Limits sound like they need something clever. For a polynomial, they do not.

A limit asks where the function is HEADING as x closes in on 4. Come from below: at 3 point 9, at 3 point 99, the values creep towards something. Come from above: 4 point 1, 4 point 01, they creep towards the same thing.
They agree because a polynomial has no gaps and no jumps anywhere — the graph is one unbroken curve. So where it is HEADING is simply where it IS. Substitute: 4 squared is 16, plus 4, plus 2… 22.
For a polynomial, a limit is just a substitution. The answer is 22. Polynomials have no gaps, so you can just substitute.
The integral of x to the power 4. Integrating is differentiating run backwards, so the question is really: what would I have to differentiate to GET x to the power 4?

The power rule brings the exponent down and takes one off it. Run it backwards: put one ON to the exponent first. 4 plus 1 is 5, so try x to the power 5. Differentiate that to check — it gives 5 x to the power 4. Close, but 5 times too big.

So divide by 5. The answer is x to the power 5, over 5. And one last thing: add C. Any constant differentiates to zero, so a constant could have been sitting there and left no trace. C stands for all of them at once.
Add one to the power, divide by the new power, and never forget the plus C. Add one to the power, divide by the new power, add C.
